tagline: Home of the giant sable antelope
overview:
Angola stretches along the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa, covering about 1.25 million square kilometers, nearly twice the size of Texas. Its capital, Luanda, is a bustling port city of high-rise towers and crowded neighborhoods that is one of the largest cities in Africa. Around 36 million people live in Angola, making it the most populous Portuguese-speaking country on the continent. A small separate piece of the country, Cabinda, lies to the north, cut off from the rest by a strip of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Angola is rich in oil and diamonds, and the money they bring has built gleaming office blocks in Luanda, although many Angolans still live in poverty in the countryside and in city outskirts. The country is a republic with an elected president and parliament. After decades of war that ended in 2002, Angolans have been rebuilding roads, railways, and schools, and a young population, more than half under 20, is shaping a fast-changing nation known for its music and dance.
landAndNature: From a narrow, dry coastal plain the land climbs steeply to a vast central highland, the planalto, where most people farm. Mount Moco, the highest point, reaches about 2,600 meters. Great rivers begin here: the Cuanza flows to the Atlantic, the Cubango wanders southeast to feed Botswana's Okavango Delta, and the mighty Congo River forms part of the northern border. In the far south the Namib Desert crosses in from Namibia, home to the welwitschia, a plant with two leathery leaves that can live for more than a thousand years. The Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River plunge over 100 meters in a wide curtain. Angola's national symbol is the giant sable antelope, with curved horns over 1.5 meters long, which was feared extinct until it was rediscovered in 2004.
peopleAndCulture: The largest groups are the Ovimbundu, Ambundu, and Bakongo, and languages such as Umbundu, Kimbundu, and Kikongo are spoken alongside official Portuguese. Most Angolans are Christian. A typical meal centers on funge, a smooth porridge of cassava or corn, served with muamba de galinha, chicken simmered in palm oil with okra. Angola's musical influence reaches far beyond its borders: semba, an older dance style, is an ancestor of Brazil's samba, and kizomba, a smooth partner dance from the 1980s, is now taught in dance schools worldwide. Basketball is a national strength, with the men's team winning the African championship 11 times, and the soccer team is nicknamed the Palancas Negras, the black sables.
history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled here over a thousand years ago and built kingdoms such as Kongo and Ndongo, whose rulers held the title ngola, the source of the country's name. Portuguese ships arrived in 1483, and Luanda was founded in 1576. For about 300 years Angola was one of the main sources of enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic, especially to Brazil. Queen Nzinga of Ndongo fought the Portuguese for decades in the 1600s. A war of independence began in 1961, and Portugal withdrew in 1975. Almost immediately a civil war broke out between rival movements backed by Cold War powers; it lasted 27 years, killed hundreds of thousands, and left the land littered with mines. Peace came in 2002, followed by an oil boom.
funFacts: Angola's flag shows half a cogwheel, a machete, and a star, symbols chosen when the country became independent in 1975.
The kizomba dance craze that fills clubs from Lisbon to Los Angeles began in the neighborhoods of Luanda.
The giant sable antelope survived the civil war hidden in a remote forest and was confirmed alive by camera traps in 2004.
The welwitschia of Angola's Namib Desert grows only two leaves in its entire life, which can last over a thousand years.
Kalandula Falls is about 400 meters wide, making it one of the largest waterfalls in Africa by volume.
